questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Moment of Inertia Given a Description of a Mass Density Function
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $y$-axis.
Find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|x|=kx,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}kx\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k({\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y) \\  & =k{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(\frac{1}{2}-0)(2-0) \\  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=M$ and hence $\lambda (x,y)=kx=Mx.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{4}y+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =M(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{11M}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Moment of Inertia Given a Description of a Mass Density Function
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072087/assets/a39a8998e4e1ae9f6ed8095b124ba31db5f3b4ffb699db815ef03144479f798c.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant enclosed by the line $y=2-2x$ and the coordinate axes. The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $x$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2-2x},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072087/assets/aad890b85e9984fdab58a2fa15e00fad4b384a086346ad77f49f68a746e73b3a.png)

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|y|=ky,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2-2x}ky\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2-2x}y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2-2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}(2-2x)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2k{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2k{[-\frac{1}{3}(1-x)^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2k\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3M}{2}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=ky=\frac{3M}{2}y.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2-2x}{y}^{2}(y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2-2x}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2-2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}(2-2x)^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6M{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6M{[-\frac{1}{5}(1-x)^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6M\cdot \frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{6M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Moment of Inertia of a Lamina With Uniform Mass Density
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 3},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{9}\cdot 27 \\  & =3M.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $3M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Moments of Inertia Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072087/assets/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt[5]{2}$ and the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15y.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072087/assets/3f9732e0b81ba2e171a0464996e7b0d27aa47a0b32da59fa40cbba0cdbf8402a.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ bounded by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=2,$ as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}kr\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}k{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{14\pi k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr=\frac{3M}{14\pi }r.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{3M}{14\pi }r\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{93M}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$
